courses.title: Medical-Surgical Nursing I
courses.description: Fluid and electrolyte care, peri-operative nursing, wound care, and the nursing management of respiratory and cardiovascular conditions.

topics.title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid–Base Nursing
topics.summary: Assessing hydration, IV fluid therapy, fluid balance charting and electrolyte imbalances.

material.heading: Assessment and IV therapy
material.body: Dehydration signs: thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, tachycardia, hypotension, reduced urine output (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) and concentrated urine. Fluid overload signs: oedema, raised JVP, breathlessness, basal crackles, weight gain. An accurate fluid balance (intake–output) chart and daily weights guide therapy. Crystalloids: 0.9% sodium chloride (isotonic, resuscitation), Ringer's lactate/Hartmann's (balanced), 5% dextrose (effectively free water — not for resuscitation), dextrose–saline. Colloids expand plasma volume. Nurses check the prescription, fluid, rate, cannula site (phlebitis: redness, pain, swelling — remove cannula) and watch for infiltration and overload. Drip rate (drops/min) = volume (mL) × drop factor ÷ time (min).
keyPoints: Dehydration: dry mucosa, poor turgor, low urine

material.heading: Electrolytes
material.body: Normal values: sodium 135–145 mmol/L; potassium 3.5–5.0 mmol/L; calcium 2.2–2.6 mmol/L. Hypokalaemia (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea) causes muscle weakness, ileus and arrhythmias (flat T waves, U waves). Hyperkalaemia (renal failure, excess supplements, haemolysed sample) causes peaked T waves and cardiac arrest risk. IV potassium must never be given as a bolus; it must be diluted and infused slowly (usually ≤ 10 mmol/h peripherally) with cardiac monitoring for high rates. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion and seizures; rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
keyPoints: Never give IV potassium as a bolus

questions.stem: Which is a sign of fluid overload?
questions.explanation: Excess fluid causes pulmonary and systemic congestion.

questions.stem: The IV fluid of choice for initial resuscitation of hypovolaemia is:
questions.explanation: Isotonic crystalloids expand the extracellular volume.

questions.stem: Normal serum potassium is:
questions.explanation: Normal potassium is 3.5–5.0 mmol/L.

questions.stem: Potassium chloride must never be given:
questions.explanation: A bolus can cause fatal cardiac arrest.

questions.stem: A cannula site that is red, painful and swollen along the vein suggests:
questions.explanation: Remove the cannula and document.

questions.stem: Urine output below which value in adults suggests inadequate renal perfusion?
questions.explanation: Output < 0.5 mL/kg/h is oliguria.

questions.stem: 1,000 mL of fluid is to run over 8 hours with a 20 drops/mL giving set. The rate is about:
Flat T waves and U waves on the ECG suggest:
questions.explanation: Low potassium alters repolarisation.

topics.title: Peri-operative Nursing
topics.summary: Pre-operative preparation, intra-operative safety and post-operative care and complications.

material.heading: Pre- and intra-operative care
material.body: Pre-operative preparation: informed consent (obtained by the surgeon), identification band, allergy check, baseline vital signs and investigations, fasting (commonly no solids for 6 hours and clear fluids up to 2 hours before anaesthesia, per local policy), skin preparation, removal of jewellery, dentures and nail polish, bladder emptying, pre-medication as prescribed, thromboprophylaxis (stockings, early mobilisation, heparin) and psychological preparation. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (sign in, time out, sign out) prevents wrong-site surgery and retained instruments; swab and instrument counts are performed.
keyPoints: Fasting: solids 6 h, clear fluids 2 h
WHO checklist: sign in, time out, sign out

material.heading: Post-operative care
material.body: In the recovery room, maintain the airway (the commonest early risk — tongue falling back, laryngospasm), monitor vital signs, oxygen saturation, level of consciousness, pain, wound drainage and urine output. Complications: primary haemorrhage (during surgery), reactionary haemorrhage (within 24 hours as BP rises or a ligature slips), secondary haemorrhage (7–10 days, from infection); atelectasis (early post-operative fever, first 48 hours — prevented by deep breathing and early mobilisation); wound infection (day 3–7); deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism; urinary retention; paralytic ileus; post-operative nausea and vomiting. Early mobilisation, adequate analgesia and deep-breathing exercises prevent many complications.
keyPoints: Early mobilisation prevents DVT and chest infection

questions.stem: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist has three phases: sign in, time out and:
questions.explanation: Sign out occurs before the patient leaves theatre.

questions.stem: Written informed consent for surgery should be obtained by the:
questions.explanation: The operating surgeon explains risks and obtains consent.

questions.stem: The priority nursing concern in the immediate post-anaesthesia period is:
questions.explanation: Airway obstruction is the most immediate threat.

questions.stem: Fever within 48 hours after abdominal surgery is most commonly due to:
questions.explanation: Collapsed alveoli are the commonest early cause.

questions.stem: Bleeding 7–10 days after surgery, usually due to infection, is:
questions.explanation: Infection erodes vessels, causing secondary haemorrhage.

questions.stem: The best measure to prevent post-operative deep vein thrombosis is:
questions.explanation: Mobilisation and anticoagulant/mechanical prophylaxis reduce DVT.

questions.stem: Before surgery, patients should remove:
questions.explanation: These interfere with safety, monitoring or the airway.

questions.stem: Deep-breathing and coughing exercises after surgery mainly prevent:
options: Pulmonary complications such as atelectasis and pneumonia
questions.explanation: They re-expand alveoli and clear secretions.

topics.title: Wound Care and Infection Prevention in Surgery
topics.summary: Wound healing, types of wounds and dressings, surgical site infection and pressure ulcers.

material.heading: Healing
material.body: Wound healing phases: haemostasis, inflammation (days 0–4), proliferation (granulation tissue, angiogenesis, epithelialisation — days 4–21) and maturation/remodelling (up to 1–2 years). Healing by primary intention: clean wound edges brought together (sutured surgical wound) — minimal scarring. Secondary intention: wound left open to granulate (infected or large tissue loss) — more scarring. Tertiary (delayed primary) intention: closure after a delay once infection is controlled. Factors delaying healing: infection, poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), diabetes, smoking, steroids, anaemia, old age, poor blood supply and pressure.

material.heading: Wound management
material.body: Aseptic (non-touch) technique is used for dressings. Normal saline is a safe cleansing solution. Choose dressings to keep a moist wound environment, absorb exudate and protect: films (superficial), hydrocolloids, hydrogels (dry necrotic wounds), alginates and foams (heavy exudate). Surgical site infection signs: redness, warmth, swelling, pain, pus, fever and wound breakdown, usually 3–7 days after surgery; take a swab for culture. Wound dehiscence (separation of layers) and evisceration are emergencies — cover with sterile moist saline dressings and call the surgeon. Pressure ulcers are staged 1 (non-blanching erythema) to 4 (full-thickness loss exposing bone/tendon).
keyPoints: Dehiscence: cover with sterile saline-soaked dressing

questions.stem: A clean surgical incision closed with sutures heals by:
questions.explanation: Edges are approximated with minimal tissue loss.

questions.stem: Granulation tissue forms during the ___ phase.
questions.explanation: New capillaries and fibroblasts form granulation tissue.

questions.stem: Which factor delays wound healing?
questions.explanation: Hyperglycaemia impairs immunity and repair.

questions.stem: The solution most commonly used for routine wound cleansing is:
questions.explanation: Saline is non-toxic to healing tissues.

questions.stem: If abdominal wound dehiscence with evisceration occurs, the nurse should first:
options: Cover with sterile saline-moistened dressings and call the surgeon
questions.explanation: Moist sterile cover protects the viscera.

questions.stem: Surgical site infections usually become apparent:
options: On the day of surgery only
questions.explanation: Signs typically appear 3–7 days post-operatively.

questions.stem: A stage 1 pressure ulcer is characterised by:
questions.explanation: Stage 1: intact skin with persistent redness.

questions.stem: Vitamin C is important for wound healing because it is needed for:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is needed for collagen hydroxylation.

topics.title: Nursing Care of Respiratory Conditions
topics.summary: Oxygen therapy, asthma, pneumonia, tuberculosis and chest drain care.

material.heading: Oxygen and airway care
material.body: Oxygen is a drug and must be prescribed with target saturations: usually 94–98%, or 88–92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. COPD). Delivery: nasal cannula (1–4 L/min, ~24–40%), simple face mask (5–10 L/min), Venturi mask (fixed, precise concentrations — preferred in COPD), non-rebreather mask with reservoir (10–15 L/min, up to ~85–90%). Position breathless patients upright (high Fowler's). Humidify high-flow oxygen. Observe for fire risk — no smoking or naked flames. Suctioning should be brief (≤ 10–15 seconds) with pre-oxygenation.

material.heading: Specific conditions
material.body: Asthma: teach correct inhaler technique (spacer use), recognise severe attack (inability to complete sentences, SpO2 < 92%, silent chest = life-threatening), give nebulised salbutamol and oxygen as prescribed. Pneumonia: monitor vital signs, oxygen, fluids, antibiotics, chest physiotherapy, positioning. Tuberculosis: DOTS (directly observed treatment, short-course), airborne precautions until non-infectious (usually after about 2 weeks of effective treatment), adherence counselling, nutrition, contact tracing, and HIV testing. Underwater-seal chest drain care: keep the drainage bottle below chest level, check swinging (oscillation) and bubbling, never clamp routinely, keep the tubing secure.
keyPoints: TB: DOTS, airborne precautions, contact tracing
Chest drain bottle below chest level

questions.stem: Target oxygen saturation for most acutely ill adults is:
questions.explanation: 94–98% unless at risk of hypercapnia.

questions.stem: The device that gives precise oxygen concentrations, preferred in COPD, is the:
questions.explanation: Venturi masks deliver fixed FiO2.

questions.stem: A 'silent chest' during an asthma attack indicates:
questions.explanation: Very little air movement means severe obstruction.

questions.stem: DOTS in tuberculosis control stands for:
questions.explanation: Treatment is observed to ensure adherence.

questions.stem: An underwater-seal chest drain bottle should be kept:
options: Below the level of the chest
Above the level of the chest
questions.explanation: This prevents backflow into the pleural space.

questions.stem: Oscillation (swinging) of fluid in the chest drain tube with respiration indicates:
options: A patent drain connected to the pleural space
The lung has fully re-expanded and must be removed
questions.explanation: Swinging shows the system is patent.

questions.stem: Suctioning of the airway should last no more than about:
questions.explanation: Prolonged suction causes hypoxia.

questions.stem: A patient receiving oxygen should be educated that:
options: Oxygen can be adjusted freely by relatives
Oxygen supports combustion, so no smoking or open flames
questions.explanation: Oxygen greatly increases fire risk.

topics.title: Nursing Care of Cardiovascular Conditions
topics.summary: Hypertension, heart failure, myocardial infarction, anticoagulant therapy and shock.

material.heading: Hypertension and heart failure
material.body: Hypertension is common in Nigeria and often asymptomatic. Nursing care: accurate BP measurement (correct cuff size, seated rest for 5 minutes, arm at heart level), lifestyle education (salt reduction, weight loss, exercise, limiting alcohol, stopping smoking), and adherence to antihypertensives. Heart failure: monitor daily weight (gain of > 2 kg in 3 days suggests fluid retention), fluid balance, oedema and breathlessness; position upright; restrict salt and sometimes fluid; give diuretics as prescribed and monitor potassium; watch for digoxin toxicity (nausea, visual disturbance, bradycardia — check apical pulse and withhold if < 60/min per protocol).
keyPoints: Digoxin: check apical pulse; toxicity signs

material.heading: Acute coronary syndrome and anticoagulation
material.body: Chest pain suggestive of myocardial infarction (central, crushing, radiating to arm/jaw, with sweating) requires immediate ECG, oxygen if saturation low, aspirin (chewed) and nitrates as prescribed, analgesia (morphine), and continuous monitoring for arrhythmias. Anticoagulants: heparin (monitor aPTT for unfractionated heparin; antidote protamine) and warfarin (monitor INR; antidote vitamin K; avoid drug interactions and alcohol, keep dietary vitamin K consistent). Observe for bleeding (gums, urine, stools). Shock: position flat with legs raised (unless contraindicated), oxygen, IV access and fluids as prescribed, monitor vital signs and urine output.
keyPoints: MI: ECG, aspirin, nitrates, oxygen if hypoxic

questions.stem: Before measuring blood pressure, the patient should rest seated for about:
questions.explanation: Rest gives a reliable resting reading.

questions.stem: A weight gain of more than 2 kg in 3 days in a heart failure patient suggests:
questions.explanation: Rapid weight gain reflects fluid accumulation.

questions.stem: Before giving digoxin, the nurse should check the:
questions.explanation: Withhold if the pulse is below the set threshold (often 60/min).

questions.stem: Warfarin therapy is monitored using the:
questions.explanation: The INR reflects warfarin's effect.

questions.stem: The antidote for heparin overdose is:
questions.explanation: Protamine neutralises heparin.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected myocardial infarction is usually given:
questions.explanation: Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation early.

questions.stem: Which lifestyle advice most directly helps lower blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Salt reduction lowers blood pressure.

questions.stem: Signs of digoxin toxicity include:
questions.explanation: Classic signs include GI upset, yellow-green vision and bradyarrhythmias.
